IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT
NAINITAL
Criminal Appeal No. 71 of 2003
Ashish .......... Appellant
 versus
State of Uttaranchal .......... Respondents

Mr. Rajat Mittal, Amicus Curiae, present for the Appellant.
Mr. Sohail Ahmad Siddiqui, learned AGA, assisted by Ms. Meena Vohara,
Brief Holder, present for the State.

JUDGMENT
U.C. Dhyani, J. (Oral)
 PW 1 Anuj Kumar (complainant/injured) lodged a
first information report against the accused-appellant Ashish on
28.07.2000 at reporting outpost Rani Pokhari, District Dehradun
for the offence under Sections 307, 504 and 506 IPC. The
incident allegedly took place on 28.07.2000, at 8:30 am, and the
first information report was lodged promptly on the selfsame day
at 9:00 am. The distance between the place of incident and the
PS concerned was 200 meters only. The informant thus lost no
time in promptly lodging the FIR. After the investigation, a
charge-sheet under Sections 307, 504, 506 IPC and Section 25/4
Arms Act was submitted against the accused (appellant herein).
2. When the trial began and prosecution opened it's
case, charges for the offences punishable under Section 307 IPC
and Section 25/4 Arms Act were framed against the accused,

2
who pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. PW 1 Anuj Kumar
(injured), PW 2 Jai Prakash, PW 3 Yashpal Singh, PW 4
Ramesh Kothari, PW 5 Jugul Kishor, PW 6 Head Constable Shri
Krishna Gupta, PW 7 Doctor M.S.Rawat, PW 8 SI Vivekanand
Tiwari, PW 9 Rajesh Kumar, PW 10 SI Mahendra Singh and
PW 11 SI N.D. Thakur were examined on behalf of the
prosecution. Incriminating evidence was put to the accused
person under Section 313 Cr.P.C., in reply to which he said that
he was falsely implicated in the case. After considering the
evidence on record, learned Additional Sessions Judge/Ist FTC/
Special Judge, CBI, Dehradun, held the accused guilty of the
offence punishable under Section 307 IPC and directed him to
undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years along with fine of
Rs. 2000/-, in default of which, he was directed to undergo three
months' further rigorous imprisonment. He was also convicted
Section 4/25 (1) (B)(b) Arms Act and was directed to undergo
two years' rigorous imprisonment along with a fine of Rs. 500/-,
in default of which, he was further directed to undergo one
month's rigorous imprisonment. Aggrieved against the judgment
and order dated 19.02.2003, present criminal appeal was
preferred on behalf of the convict-appellant.
3. Prosecution led the evidence through PW 1 and PW
3. Both were the eyewitnesses, in addition to the fact that PW 1
was also the informant. PW 1, in his examination-in-chief, stated
that on 28.07.2000 at around 8:30 am, accused-appellant met
him near Mukesh Lakhera's shop. Since the accused-appellant
belonged to neighboring village, therefore, PW 1 knew him
personally before the alleged incident. Accused-appellant
stopped the motorcycle of PW 1 and said that PW 1 was
becoming the leader and inflicted the blow of knife on the right
side of chest of PW 1. Injured tried to stop the blow, as a

3
consequence of which, he sustained injuries on his palm. After
inflicting blows of knife, accused appellant threatened PW 1
with dire consequences and fled away. Ramesh Kothari and
Yashpal came on the place of incident. PW 1 rang his brother
Jay Prakash, who wrote the complaint on the dictation of PW 1.
PW 1 also proved his complaint (Ext. Ka-1). Wearing apparels,
namely, shirt (material ext. -1) and undershirt (material ext. -2)
of the injured were also produced before the trial court. On the
previous day of the incident, an altercation took place between
the accused-appellant and co-villagers of PW 1, in which
accused-appellant threatened that whosoever will come to Rani
Pokhari, he will be assaulted and will be dealt with
appropriately.
4. In his cross-examination, PW 1 said that when
accused-appellant stopped his motorcycle, Rani Pokhari bazar
was opened. Ramesh Kothari and Yashpal belonged to PW 1's
village. Accused-appellant stopped PW 1 near Mukesh
Lakhera's shop. Accused was resident of adjacent village. PW 1
had no enmity with the appellant before this incident. PW 1
further stated that none else except Ramesh Kothari and Yashpal
came to save PW 1, in as much as, everybody was frightened
with him (appellant). He was in the habit of assaulting the
villagers. There was a distance of one kilometer between Dandi,
the village of PW 1 and Rani Pokhari, where the incident took
place. PW 1's brother came about ten minutes later when PW 1
rang him up. Although Rani Pokhari police outpost was situated
at a distance of 10 meters from the place of incident, but no
police personnel was present when such incident took place.
Yashpal and Ramesh Kothari saw the incident. Ramesh Kothari
was the tempo driver and Yashpal was a tractor driver. In this
way, nothing came in the cross-examination of PW 1 to suggest

4
that he was telling a lie. Nothing material came in his cross-examination to treat his testimony with suspicion.
5. PW 2 wrote the complaint (Ext. Ka-1) on the
dictation of injured (PW 1). He was not an eyewitness.
6. PW 3 said that he saw the altercation taking place
between the appellant and the injured. He said that he did not
hear the abuses being hurled by the appellant on PW 1. PW 3
also did not see any injury on the person of PW 1. In the cross-examination, PW 3 said that he was a resident of village Dandi.
He had gone to Rani Pokhari for some work. He reached Rani
Pokhari at around 9:30 am. He was standing at chauraha
(intersection). He did not see the weapon by which appellant
assaulted the injured. He only saw scuffle taking place between
the appellant and the injured. He did not see that the appellant
inflicted blow of knife on injured.
7. PW 4 did not support the prosecution story and was
declared hostile. PW 5 was the signatory to the taking into
possession of the wearing apparels of PW 1. PW 6 was a formal
witness, who proved chik FIR (Ext. Ka-3), which was lodged on
the basis of complaint (Ext. Ka-1). An entry of the same was
made in G.D. (Ext. Ka-4).
8. PW 7 was the medical officer, who examined the
injuries of PW 1 on 28.07.2000, at 11:30 am. He found
following injuries on the person of injured:
i. Incised wound obliquely placed over left wrist on front
aspect 3 cm x 0.5 cm x skin deep. Margins clean & sharp.
Clotted blood present on the wound. Wound stitching

5
from the centre of the wrist & tapers towards the medical
side.
ii. Incised wound 8 cm x 05 cm x skin deep obliquely placed
over chest right side 3 cm below right nipple. Wound
covered with clotted fresh blood. Margins are clean and
sharp. Wound started from lateral side and tapers on
medical side.
iii. Oblique abrasion 1.25 cm x 0.25 cm covered with blood
clot placed over chest right side in auxiliary line 4 cm
lateral to injury no. 2.
iv. Incised wound 1.25 cm x 0.25 x skin deep clean and sharp
margins.
9. PW 7, while proving the injury report (Ext. Ka-5),
opined that all the injuries were caused by sharp and hard object
and were simple in nature. The duration of such injuries was
fresh. The oral testimony of PW 1 was thus corroborated by PW
7.
10. PW 8 was the police personnel in whose presence
the prohibited knife was found from the possession of accused-appellant. Recovery memo (Ext. Ka-6) was prepared by him.
Ext. Ka-7 was memo of arrest and Ext. Ka-8 was the memo of
information of arrest to his family members. Prohibited knife
was proved as material Ext. 1. PW 9 also was the witness of
recovery of knife from the accused-appellant. PW 10 was a
formal witness, who registered chik FIR (Ext. Ka- 9) under
Section 25/4 Arms Act and entry of the same in G.D. (Ext. Ka-10). PW 11 was the investigating officer, who submitted the
charge-sheet (Ext. Ka-12) and also proved the charge-sheet (Ext.
Ka-14) under Section 25/4 Arms Act.

6
11. DW 1 Mukesh Lakhera was the STD owner, in
whose vicinity the incident allegedly took place, but DW 1
denied such incident having taken place near his STD (shop). He
also stated that no scuffle took place between the appellant and
the injured in his presence. DW 1 was known to both the
appellant and the injured. He further stated that appellant
brought him to the Court to depose in his favour. DW 1's
evidence was in the form of negative evidence.
12. The testimony of PW 1 was thus supported by PW 3,
who although did not belong to the village where the incident
took place, but, nevertheless, he was living at a distance of 1 or
1 1⁄2 kilometers from the village, where the incident took place.
He was a tractor driver, who went to clinic of a doctor in the
morning. He was standing on chauraha (intersection) of the
road, wherefrom he saw that a scuffle was taking place between
the appellant and the injured. Although he did not see that
appellant inflicted blow of knife on the injured, yet the fact
remains that he saw the incident (of altercation and scuffle).
There are persons who are keen observers and at the same time,
there are persons who are casual observers. PW 3 appears to be a
casual observer, for he was not that attentive to have seen the
incident in it's totality. There remains no doubt that he saw
scuffle taking place between the appellant and the injured. The
testimony of PW 1 has been discussed by this Court in one of the
foregoing paragraphs of this judgment, to infer that the
testimony of PW 1 could not be treated with suspicion. His
testimony was acceptable. PW 1 did not take a false plea that
appellant inflicted blow of knife upon him on account of
previous enmity. Accused, in his statement under Section 313
Cr.P.C., also did not say that he was falsely implicated in this
case. There was, therefore, no enmity between the appellant and

7
the injured prior to the incident in question. It is settled law that
the motive goes into oblivion when the direct evidence comes to
the fore. The testimony of PW 1 was supported by PW 7 that the
medical officer found incised wounds on the person of the
injured. All the injuries sustained by PW 1 were caused by sharp
and hard object. The testimony of PW 1 was thus corroborated
by PW 7 and by PW 3, to certain extent. Even if it be conceded
for the sake of arguments that PW 3 was a chance witness, the
fact remains that PW 1 was supported by PW 7. The testimony
of PW 1 was scrutinized by this Court with vehemence, only to
come to the conclusion that his testimony was an acceptable
piece of evidence, which was duly corroborated by the testimony
of PW 7. The peripheral evidence also lends support to the
prosecution story.
13. Prosecution story was thus proved against the
accused-appellant, but only in respect of offence under Section
324 IPC, as also (Section 25/4 Arms Act), in as much as, PW 7
nowhere stated that the injuries sustained by PW 1 were
grievous or fatal in nature. All that PW 7 said was that the
injuries sustained by the injured were caused by sharp and hard
object and were simple in nature.
14. Criminal appeal is, therefore, partly allowed.
Conviction and sentence awarded to the appellant under Section
307 IPC is set aside. The conviction under Section 25/4 Arms
Act is however, affirmed. Instead of convicting the appellant
under Section 307 IPC, he is convicted under Section 324 IPC
and is directed to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of
2 1⁄2 years along with a fine of Rs. 2000/-, in default of payment
of which, the appellant shall further undergo rigorous
imprisonment for three months. Both the sentences (under

8
Section 324 IPC and Section 25/4 Arms Act) shall run
concurrently. If the fine is realized from the appellant, the same
shall be awarded to PW 1 as compensation under Section 357
Cr.P.C. The accused-appellant is on bail. His bail is cancelled.
He is directed to surrender forthwith before the Court below to
serve out the sentence as is modified by this Court.
15. Let a copy of this judgment along with lower court
record be sent to the Court below for compliance.
 (U.C. Dhyani, J.)
Dt. December 17, 2013
Kaushal
